topic: Polymorphism and Dynamic Binding with Virtual Functions
explanation: Polymorphism, meaning "many forms", allows you to treat objects of different classes in a uniform way.  This is crucial for building flexible and extensible code.  In C++, dynamic binding (runtime polymorphism) is achieved using virtual functions.  A virtual function is declared using the `virtual` keyword in the base class. When a virtual function is called through a pointer or reference to a base class, the correct version of the function (the one defined in the derived class) is executed at runtime. This enables you to write code that can work with objects of various derived classes without needing to know their specific types at compile time.  A common pitfall is forgetting the `virtual` keyword in the base class, leading to static binding (the base class function is always called).
code_example: virtual double getArea() = 0; // Pure virtual function, making Shape abstract
double getArea() override { return 3.14159 * radius_ * radius_; }
void draw() override { std::cout << "Drawing a circle\n"; }
Rectangle(double width, double height) : width_(width), height_(height) {}
double getArea() override { return width_ * height_; }
void draw() override { std::cout << "Drawing a rectangle\n"; }
example_explanation: This example demonstrates polymorphism with shapes.  We define an abstract base class `Shape` with pure virtual functions `getArea` and `draw`.  `Circle` and `Rectangle` inherit from `Shape` and provide concrete implementations.  The `main` function uses pointers to `Shape` to work with objects of different types, illustrating dynamic binding. The area is calculated and each shape is drawn correctly at runtime, showcasing the flexibility and power of polymorphism. This pattern is useful in scenarios involving graphical user interfaces, game development, and any situation where you need to handle diverse object types uniformly.
